cells.tense: You are standing at the work right now, and the work is holding.
cells.act: hold space for what someone feels without fixing it
cells.ask: When someone hands you something they're feeling, don't reach for a solution. Stay with it. The staying is the reply — nothing has to be fixed for it to count.
cells.core:
You can build and you can hold, and right now they're the same act. You stand in the stripped-down pattern of things — how a load moves, where a wall has to go — and you're not trying to prove the pattern is right, just working it. Where you bend toward it, somebody comes to you with something they can't carry and you don't take it off them. You stay beside it. Strength that doesn't need to own what it protects.

You've made something that doesn't need re-convincing every week. What could come next is connection without losing the frame — someone comes close and you stay whole in it. The practice: when feeling shows up in your work or your home, hold it without fixing it. Sit with what they bring. You'll know it's working because you won't be managing them. No push required. They will move through it, and you'll still be beside them.
cells.sheetLine: Strength that doesn't crush what it holds.
cells.verb: building what holds up under weight
cells.place: in the pattern stripped of its surface picture

cells.tense: You'll have the whole thing built before anyone has agreed it's needed.
cells.act: weigh what it costs them against what it gives
cells.ask: Before you settle the next move, put what it costs the person beside you on one side of the scale, and decide with that number instead of against it.
cells.core:
You can see the finished shape before anyone else has started, and you are already there in your mind — braced for a load that isn't on you yet. The pattern in your head is clear enough that the actual situation looks like an obstacle to getting it done, and that is what the others meet. You're holding the structure so tight that the structure is what they get, not you. It isn't force for no reason. The ending is already set, and waiting feels like losing what you've built.

Let fairness be the judge instead of the blueprint. When you're about to move on something, stop and weigh what it will cost the person it touches against what it gives, and decide by that number rather than by the plan. And if the share comes out uneven, you'll see it once, at the end, instead of at every turn. That's enough correction for one stretch.
cells.sheetLine: You're building at people instead of with them.
cells.verb: building what holds up under weight

cells.tense: You were holding the frame, and now you're standing at a door that closed behind you.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Take something you've already finished — actually complete — and set it down this week. Let the next step come after that.
cells.core:
The pattern is there — a frame that holds, a load that lands where you put it. But you've stopped stepping into new ones, and the strength has gone still. It's not that you can't. Staying put has gotten easier than arriving. What's built looks too heavy to move, so it doesn't move. The frame still stands. The rooms are quiet.

What is called for isn't more effort. Let go of something finished. Take one project, one job, one commitment you already brought to its end — and set it down completely this week. Take the step that comes after it. You'll know the old work was done when you can leave it alone without checking back. What you keep is the part still growing. What you set down has already paid you.
cells.sheetLine: What you've finished is holding you at the door.

cells.tense: You're already writing at the work, and your hand is off the page.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Start something this week for no other reason than that it's interesting — no plan, no deadline, nobody has to see it. Catch yourself doing it.
cells.core:
You steer by a pattern you can read, and if someone asked you'd say it's just how things are. Where the wall goes, where the load lands — the eye is clean and reliable, and it doesn't feel like a decision. So when the result comes out right, you file it under the way the work works. Your name doesn't go on the clear eye. The clearer it gets, the less you notice the eye has an owner.

You can start smaller than the whole plan. Find one direction that has no destination yet and begin it this week just to begin it. No deadline, no audience. When you catch yourself wanting to see how it ends before you start, that's the old pattern. Let the beginning be enough. The spark is yours even when you don't claim it.
